claims.text: A stable protective oxide scale is the primary mechanism governing the high-temperature wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings.
Thermally activated oxidation of FeNiCrCoCu occurs in the proposed 400–600°C range.
The resulting oxide layer acts as a hard barrier that reduces material removal under sliding loads.
The initial material is a FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating on a conventional metal substrate.
The baseline coating has a typical microstructure and grain size resulting from room-temperature deposition.
Heating the coating in ambient air before wear testing will produce a thermally grown oxide layer.
The thermally grown scale is likely to contain mixed oxides of Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu.
The thermally grown oxide scale will be mechanically robust and hard.
Oxidation of FeNiCrCoCu at elevated temperature produces a thin, adherent scale.
The oxide scale enhances surface hardness.
The oxide scale acts sacrificially and dissipates mechanical stresses during sliding.
The oxide scale prevents or delays exposure of the underlying substrate.
Pre-oxidized coatings will have lower wear rates than as-deposited coatings during otherwise identical tests at 400–600°C.
Pre-oxidized coatings will develop shallower wear scars than as-deposited coatings.
The protective oxide layer will be detectable by XPS or SEM-EDS mapping.
Oxide-scale formation will correlate with increased high-temperature surface hardness and improved wear resistance.
The proposed mechanism applies within a temperature range of 400–600°C under sliding-contact loading.
The mechanism may not apply at room temperature because oxidation is minimal there.
The composition and mechanical properties of the oxide scale may vary with processing conditions.
